## Agent terminal keybindings (Cursor docs)

### In-editor terminal prompt bar (Cmd K)

From [Keyboard Shortcuts | Cursor Docs](https://cursor.com/docs/reference/keyboard-shortcuts):

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| **Cmd K** | Open terminal prompt bar |
| **Cmd Return** | Run generated command |
| **Escape** | Accept command |

### CLI agent (terminal `cursor agent`)

From [Using Agent in CLI](https://cursor.com/docs/cli/using):

| Shortcut | Action |
|----------|--------|
| **Shift+Enter** | Newline (multi-line) — iTerm2, Ghostty, Kitty, Warp, Zed |
| **Ctrl+J** or **\+Enter** | Newline (works in all terminals, including tmux/screen) |
| **Ctrl+D** | Exit CLI |
| **Shift+Tab** | Rotate modes (Agent, Plan, Ask) |
| **Arrow Up** | Previous messages |
| **Ctrl+R** | Review changes; then `i` for follow-up; arrows to scroll/switch files |

### Related shortcuts

- **Cmd E** — Toggle Agent layout  
- **Cmd Shift P** → “Keyboard Shortcuts” — View/remap all shortcuts  
- **Cmd R** then **Cmd S** — Open Keyboard Shortcuts

### Doc links

- Main shortcuts: https://cursor.com/docs/reference/keyboard-shortcuts  
- CLI usage & input shortcuts: https://cursor.com/docs/cli/using  
- CLI terminal setup (newlines): https://cursor.com/docs/cli/reference/terminal-setup  
- Customization: https://cursor.com/help/customization/keyboard-shortcuts  

All of these can be changed in **Cursor → Keyboard Shortcuts** (or Command Palette → “Keyboard Shortcuts”).

## 1. **What was added**

In your **keybindings.json** you now have:

- **Shift+Cmd+[** → `workbench.action.terminal.focusPreviousGroup`
- **Shift+Cmd+]** → `workbench.action.terminal.focusNextGroup`

Both use this **when** clause:

```text
terminalFocus && terminalHasBeenCreated && !terminalEditorFocus || terminalFocus && terminalProcessSupported && !terminalEditorFocus || terminalFocus && !terminalEditorFocus
```

So you keep the default behavior for the normal terminal and **also** run these commands when focus is in any terminal that’s not the embedded terminal editor (including the agent terminal), even if `terminalHasBeenCreated` / `terminalProcessSupported` are false there.

---

## 2. **If you want “only in agent terminal”**

If you’d rather have these keys **only** in the agent terminal (and leave the default binding unchanged elsewhere):

1. **Cmd+Shift+P** → run **“Developer: Inspect Context Keys”**.
2. Focus the **agent terminal** (click into it).
3. In the Inspect UI, click on the agent terminal area.
4. In the console/output, note the context that’s **true only** when the agent terminal is focused (e.g. something like `focusedView == 'workbench.panel.terminal.agent'` or a Cursor-specific key).

Then **remove** the two entries we added and add **overrides** that only apply in the agent terminal, for example:

```json
{
  "key": "shift+cmd+[",
  "command": "workbench.action.terminal.focusPreviousGroup",
  "when": "focusedView == 'workbench.panel.agentterminal.view'"
}
```

Use the exact **when** value you see in Inspect Context Keys so the binding runs only in the agent terminal.

---

## 3. **Other “related” terminal keybindings**

If you want the same “works in agent terminal” behavior for other terminal group/tab commands, you can add the same **when** clause to:

| Key | Command |
|-----|--------|
| **Shift+Cmd+]** | `workbench.action.terminal.focusNextGroup` (already added) |
| **Ctrl+PageUp** | same as Shift+Cmd+[ (Windows/Linux) |
| **Ctrl+PageDown** | same as Shift+Cmd+] (Windows/Linux) |

For **switching terminal tabs** (not groups):

- `workbench.action.terminal.focusNext` / `workbench.action.terminal.focusPrevious`

Add those with the same **when** clause if you want them in the agent terminal as well.

After editing keybindings, reload the window (**Cmd+Shift+P** → “Developer: Reload Window”) if the new bindings don’t apply immediately.

{"url":"https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/keybindings#_default-keybindings","markdown":"Keyboard shortcuts for Visual Studio Code\n\n[VS Code February events](https://aka.ms/vscode/events)– Agent Sessions Day on Feb 19th\n\n# Keyboard shortcuts for Visual Studio Code\n\nVisual Studio Code lets you perform most tasks directly from the keyboard. This article explains how you can modify the default keyboard shortcuts that come with VS Code.\n\nNote\n\nIf you visit this page on a Mac, you will see the keyboard shortcuts for the Mac. If you visit using Windows or Linux, you will see the keys for that platform. If you need the keyboard shortcuts for another platform, hover your mouse over the key you are interested in.\n\n## Keyboard Shortcuts editor\n\nVS Code provides a rich keyboard shortcut editing experience with the Keyboard Shortcuts editor. The editor lists all available commands with and without keyboard shortcuts, and enables you to change, remove, or reset their keyboard shortcuts using the available actions. To find commands or keyboard shortcuts, use the search box and enter a command or shortcut to filter the list.\n\nTo open the Keyboard Shortcuts editor, select the File > Preferences > Keyboard Shortcuts menu, or use the Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts command (⌘K ⌘S (Windows, Linux Ctrl+K Ctrl+S)) in the Command Palette. The Keyboard Shortcuts editor opens by default in a [modal overlay](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/userinterface#_modal-editors) on top of the editor area.\n\nNote\n\nThe keyboard shortcuts match your current keyboard layout. For example, keyboard shortcut Cmd+\\ in US keyboard layout will be shown as Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Cmd+7 when the layout is changed to German. The dialog to change a keyboard shortcut assigns the correct and desired keyboard shortcut according to your keyboard layout.\n\n## Customize shortcuts for UI actions\n\nTo customize a keyboard shortcut for a UI action, right-click on any action item in your workbench, and select Configure Keybinding. This opens the Keyboard Shortcuts editor, filtered to the corresponding command. If the action has a`when` clause, it's automatically included, making it easier to set up your keyboard shortcuts just the way you need them.\n\n## Keymap extensions\n\nKeymap extensions modify the VS Code shortcuts to match those of other editors, so you don't need to learn new keyboard shortcuts.\n\nSelect the File > Preferences > Migrate Keyboard Shortcuts from... menu to get a list of popular keymap extensions. There is also a [Keymaps category](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/search?target=VSCode&amp;category=Keymaps&amp;sortBy=Installs) of extensions in the Marketplace.\n\n## Keyboard Shortcuts reference\n\nWe have a printable version of the default keyboard shortcuts. Select Help > Keyboard Shortcut Reference to display a condensed PDF version suitable for printing as an easy reference.\n\nThe following links provide access to the three platform-specific versions (US English keyboard):\n\n- [Linux](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=832144)\n- [macOS](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=832143)\n- [Windows](https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?linkid=832145)\n\n## Detecting keyboard shortcut conflicts\n\nIf you have many extensions installed or you have modified your keyboard shortcuts, there might be keyboard shortcut conflicts, where the same keyboard shortcut is mapped to multiple commands. This can result in confusing behavior, especially if different keyboard shortcuts are going in and out of scope as you move around the editor.\n\nRight-click on an item in the list of keyboard shortcuts, and select Show Same Keybindings to view all entries with the same keyboard shortcut.\n\n## Troubleshooting keyboard shortcuts\n\nTo troubleshoot keyboard shortcut problems, you can execute the command Developer: Toggle Keyboard Shortcuts Troubleshooting. This activates logging of dispatched keyboard shortcuts and opens the Output panel with the corresponding log file.\n\nYou can then press your desired keyboard shortcut and check what keyboard shortcut VS Code detects and what command is invoked.\n\nFor example, when pressing`cmd+/` in a code editor on macOS, the logging output would be:\n\n```\n[KeybindingService]: / Received  keydown event - modifiers: [meta], code: MetaLeft, keyCode: 91, key: Meta\n[KeybindingService]: | Converted keydown event - modifiers: [meta], code: MetaLeft, keyCode: 57 ('Meta')\n[KeybindingService]: \\ Keyboard event cannot be dispatched.\n[KeybindingService]: / Received  keydown event - modifiers: [meta], code: Slash, keyCode: 191, key: /\n[KeybindingService]: | Converted keydown event - modifiers: [meta], code: Slash, keyCode: 85 ('/')\n[KeybindingService]: | Resolving meta+[Slash]\n[KeybindingService]: \\ From 2 keybinding entries, matched editor.action.commentLine, when: editorTextFocus && !editorReadonly, source: built-in.\n\n```\n\nIn the example log, the first keydown event is for the`MetaLeft` key (`cmd`) and cannot be dispatched. The second keydown event is for the`Slash` key (`/`) and is dispatched as`meta+[Slash]`. There were two keyboard shortcut entries mapped from`meta+[Slash]` and the one that matched was for the command`editor.action.commentLine`, which has the`when` condition`editorTextFocus && !editorReadonly` and is a built-in keyboard shortcut entry.\n\n## Viewing modified keyboard shortcuts\n\nTo filter the list to only show the shortcuts you have modified, select the Show User Keybindings command in the More Actions (...) menu. This applies the`@source:user` filter to the Keyboard Shortcuts editor (Source is 'User').\n\n## Advanced customization\n\nVS Code keeps track of the keyboard shortcuts you have customized in the`keybindings.json` file. For advanced customization, you can also directly modify the`keybindings.json` file.\n\nTo open the`keybindings.json` file:\n\nOpen Keyboard Shortcuts editor, and then select the Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON) button on the right of the editor title bar.\n\nAlternatively, use the Open Default Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON) command in the Command Palette (⇧⌘P (Windows, Linux Ctrl+Shift+P)).\n\n## Keyboard rules\n\nA keyboard shortcut configuration in VS Code is also known as a keyboard rule. Each rule consists of the following attributes:\n\n- `when`: (optional) clause containing a boolean expression that is evaluated depending on the current context.\n- `command`: the identifier of the VS Code command to execute, for example`workbench.view.explorer` to open the Explorer view.\n- `key`: describes the pressed key(s), for example ⌘F (Windows, Linux Ctrl+F).\n\nChords (two separate keypress actions) are described by separating the two keypresses with a space. For example, Ctrl+K Ctrl+C.\n\nWhen a key is pressed, the following evaluation rules are applied:\n\n- If a rule is found and has a`command` set, the`command` is executed.\n- If a rule is found, no more rules are processed.\n- The first rule that matches both the`key` and`when` clause, is accepted.\n- Rules are evaluated from bottom to top.\n\nThe additional`keybindings.json` rules are appended at runtime to the bottom of the default rules, thus allowing them to overwrite the default rules. The`keybindings.json` file is watched by VS Code, so editing it while VS Code is running will update the rules at run-time.\n\nThe keyboard shortcuts dispatching is done by analyzing a list of rules that are expressed in JSON. Here are some examples:\n\n```\n// Keyboard shortcuts that are active when the focus is in the editor\n{ \"key\": \"home\",            \"command\": \"cursorHome\",                  \"when\": \"editorTextFocus\" },\n{ \"key\": \"shift+home\",      \"command\": \"cursorHomeSelect\",            \"when\": \"editorTextFocus\" },\n\n// Keyboard shortcuts that are complementary\n{ \"key\": \"f5\",              \"command\": \"workbench.action.debug.continue\", \"when\": \"inDebugMode\" },\n{ \"key\": \"f5\",              \"command\": \"workbench.action.debug.start\",    \"when\": \"!inDebugMode\" },\n\n// Global keyboard shortcuts\n{ \"key\": \"ctrl+f\",          \"command\": \"actions.find\" },\n{ \"key\": \"alt+left\",        \"command\": \"workbench.action.navigateBack\" },\n{ \"key\": \"alt+right\",       \"command\": \"workbench.action.navigateForward\" },\n\n// Global keyboard shortcuts using chords (two separate keypress actions)\n{ \"key\": \"ctrl+k enter\",    \"command\": \"workbench.action.keepEditor\" },\n{ \"key\": \"ctrl+k ctrl+w\",   \"command\": \"workbench.action.closeAllEditors\" },\n\n```\n\n## Accepted keys\n\nThe`key` is made up of modifiers and the key itself.\n\nThe following modifiers are accepted:\n\n| Platform | Modifiers |\n| --- | --- |\n| macOS | Ctrl+, Shift+, Alt+, Cmd+ |\n| Windows | Ctrl+, Shift+, Alt+, Win+ |\n| Linux | Ctrl+, Shift+, Alt+, Meta+ |\n\nThe following keys are accepted:\n\n- numpad_subtract, numpad_decimal, numpad_divide\n- numpad0-numpad9, numpad_multiply, numpad_add, numpad_separator\n- pausebreak, capslock, insert\n- tab, enter, escape, space, backspace, delete\n- left, up, right, down, pageup, pagedown, end, home\n- `, -, =, [, ], \\, ;, ', ,, ., /\n- f1-f19, a-z, 0-9\n\n## Command arguments\n\nYou can invoke a command with arguments. This is useful if you often perform the same operation on a specific file or folder. You can add a custom keyboard shortcut to do exactly what you want.\n\nThe following is an example overriding the Enter key to print some text:\n\n```\n{\n  \"key\": \"enter\",\n  \"command\": \"type\",\n  \"args\": { \"text\": \"Hello World\" },\n  \"when\": \"editorTextFocus\"\n}\n\n```\n\nThe`type` command will receive`{\"text\": \"Hello World\"}` as its first argument, and add \"Hello World\" to the file instead of producing the default command.\n\nFor more information on commands that take arguments, refer to [Built-in Commands](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/references/commands).\n\n## Running multiple commands\n\nA keyboard shortcut can be configured to run multiple commands sequentially by using the command`runCommands`.\n\nRun several commands without arguments:\n\nThe following example copies the current line down, marks the current line as a comment, and moves the cursor to the copied line.\n\n```\n{\n  \"key\": \"ctrl+alt+c\",\n  \"command\": \"runCommands\",\n  \"args\": {\n    \"commands\": [\n      \"editor.action.copyLinesDownAction\",\n      \"cursorUp\",\n      \"editor.action.addCommentLine\",\n      \"cursorDown\"\n    ]\n  }\n},\n\n```\n\nTo pass arguments to commands:\n\nThis example creates a new untitled TypeScript file and inserts a custom snippet.\n\n```\n{\n  \"key\": \"ctrl+n\",\n  \"command\": \"runCommands\",\n  \"args\": {\n    \"commands\": [\n      {\n        \"command\": \"workbench.action.files.newUntitledFile\",\n        \"args\": {\n          \"languageId\": \"typescript\"\n        }\n      },\n      {\n        \"command\": \"editor.action.insertSnippet\",\n        \"args\": {\n          \"langId\": \"typescript\",\n          \"snippet\": \"class ${1:ClassName} {\\n\\tconstructor() {\\n\\t\\t$0\\n\\t}\\n}\"\n        }\n      }\n    ]\n  }\n},\n\n```\n\nNote that commands run by`runCommands` receive the value of`\"args\"` as the first argument. In the previous example,`workbench.action.files.newUntitledFile` receives`{\"languageId\": \"typescript\" }` as its first and only argument.\n\nTo pass several arguments, you need to have`\"args\"` as an array:\n\n```\n{\n  \"key\": \"ctrl+shift+e\",\n  \"command\": \"runCommands\",\n  \"args\": {\n    \"commands\": [\n      {\n        // command invoked with 2 arguments: vscode.executeCommand(\"myCommand\", \"arg1\", \"arg2\")\n        \"command\": \"myCommand\",\n        \"args\": [\"arg1\", \"arg2\"]\n      }\n    ]\n  }\n}\n\n```\n\nTo pass an array as the first argument, wrap the array in another array:`\"args\": [ [1, 2, 3] ]`.\n\n## Removing a keyboard shortcut\n\nTo remove a keyboard shortcut, right-click on the entry in the Keyboard Shortcuts editor, and select Remove Keybinding.\n\nTo remove a keyboard shortcut by using the`keybindings.json` file, add a`-` to the`command` and the rule will be a removal rule.\n\nHere is an example:\n\n```\n// In Default Keyboard Shortcuts\n...\n{ \"key\": \"tab\", \"command\": \"tab\", \"when\": ... },\n{ \"key\": \"tab\", \"command\": \"jumpToNextSnippetPlaceholder\", \"when\": ... },\n{ \"key\": \"tab\", \"command\": \"acceptSelectedSuggestion\", \"when\": ... },\n...\n\n// To remove the second rule, for example, add in keybindings.json:\n{ \"key\": \"tab\", \"command\": \"-jumpToNextSnippetPlaceholder\" }\n\n\n```\n\nTo override a specific keyboard shortcut rule with an empty action, you can specify an empty command:\n\n```\n// To override and disable any `tab` keyboard shortcut, for example, add in keybindings.json:\n{ \"key\": \"tab\", \"command\": \"\" }\n\n```\n\n## Keyboard layouts\n\nNote\n\nThis section relates only to keyboard shortcuts, not to typing in the editor.\n\nKeys are string representations for virtual keys and do not necessarily relate to the produced character when they are pressed. More precisely:\n\n- etc.\n- ' for`VK_OEM_7`(`0xDE`)\n- ] for`VK_OEM_6`(`0xDD`)\n- \\ for`VK_OEM_5`(`0xDC`)\n- [ for`VK_OEM_4`(`0xDB`)\n- ` for`VK_OEM_3`(`0xC0`)\n- / for`VK_OEM_2`(`0xBF`)\n- . for`VK_OEM_PERIOD`(`0xBE`)\n- - for`VK_OEM_MINUS`(`0xBD`)\n- , for`VK_OEM_COMMA`(`0xBC`)\n- = for`VK_OEM_PLUS`(`0xBB`)\n- ; for`VK_OEM_1`(`0xBA`)\n- tab for`VK_TAB`(`0x09`)\n- Reference: [Virtual-Key Codes (Windows)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/inputdev/virtual-key-codes)\n\nDifferent keyboard layouts usually reposition these virtual keys or change the characters produced when they are pressed. When using a different keyboard layout than the standard US, Visual Studio Code does the following:\n\nAll the keyboard shortcuts are rendered in the UI using the current system's keyboard layout. For example,`Split Editor` when using a French (France) keyboard layout is now rendered as Ctrl+*:\n\nWhen editing`keybindings.json`, VS Code highlights misleading keyboard shortcuts, those that are represented in the file with the character produced under the standard US keyboard layout, but that need pressing keys with different labels under the current system's keyboard layout. For example, here is how the default keyboard shortcut rules look like when using a French (France) keyboard layout:\n\nThere is also a UI control that helps input the keyboard shortcut rule when editing`keybindings.json`. To launch the Define Keybinding control, press ⌘K ⌘K (Windows, Linux Ctrl+K Ctrl+K). The control listens for key presses and renders the serialized JSON representation in the text box and below it, the keys that VS Code has detected under your current keyboard layout. Once you've typed the key combination you want, you can press Enter and a rule snippet is inserted.\n\nNote\n\nOn Linux, VS Code detects your current keyboard layout on startup, and then caches this information. We recommend that you restart VS Code when you change your keyboard layout.\n\n## Keyboard layout-independent bindings\n\nUsing scan codes, it is possible to define keyboard shortcuts that do not change with the change of the keyboard layout. For example:\n\n```\n{ \"key\": \"cmd+[Slash]\", \"command\": \"editor.action.commentLine\", \"when\": \"editorTextFocus\" }\n\n```\n\nAccepted scan codes:\n\n- [NumpadSubtract], [NumpadDecimal], [NumpadDivide]\n- [Numpad0]-[Numpad9], [NumpadMultiply], [NumpadAdd], [NumpadComma]\n- [Pause], [CapsLock], [Insert]\n- [Tab], [Enter], [Escape], [Space], [Backspace], [Delete]\n- [ArrowLeft], [ArrowUp], [ArrowRight], [ArrowDown], [PageUp], [PageDown], [End], [Home]\n- [Backquote], [Minus], [Equal], [BracketLeft], [BracketRight], [Backslash], [Semicolon], [Quote], [Comma], [Period], [Slash]\n- [F1]-[F19], [KeyA]-[KeyZ], [Digit0]-[Digit9]\n\n## when clause contexts\n\nVS Code gives you precise control over when your keyboard shortcuts are enabled through the optional`when` clause. If your keyboard shortcut doesn't have a`when` clause, the keyboard shortcut is globally available at all times. A`when` clause evaluates to either true or false for enabling keyboard shortcuts.\n\nVS Code sets various context keys and specific values depending on what elements are visible and active in the VS Code UI. For example, the built-in Start Debugging command has the keyboard shortcut F5, which is only enabled when there is an appropriate debugger available (context`debuggersAvailable` is true) and the editor isn't in debug mode (context`inDebugMode` is false):\n\nYou can also view a keyboard shortcut's when clause directly in the default`keybinding.json`(Preferences: Open Default Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)):\n\n```\n{ \"key\": \"f5\",  \"command\": \"workbench.action.debug.start\",\n                   \"when\": \"debuggersAvailable && !inDebugMode\" },\n\n```\n\n### Conditional operators\n\nFor`when` clause conditional expressions, the following conditional operators are useful for keyboard shortcuts:\n\n| Operator | Symbol | Example |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Equality | `==` | `\"editorLangId == typescript\"` |\n| Inequality | `!=` | `\"resourceExtname != .js\"` |\n| Or | `||` | `\"isLinux``||``isWindows\"` |\n| And | `&&` | `\"textInputFocus && !editorReadonly\"` |\n| Matches | `=~` | `\"resourceScheme =~ /^untitled$|^file$/\"` |\n\nYou can find the full list of when clause conditional operators in the [when clause contexts](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/references/when-clause-contexts#_conditional-operators) reference.\n\n### Available contexts\n\nYou can find some of the available`when` clause contexts in the [when clause context reference](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/references/when-clause-contexts).\n\nThe list there isn't exhaustive and you can find other`when` clause contexts by searching and filtering in the Keyboard Shortcuts editor (Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts ) or reviewing the default`keybindings.json` file (Preferences: Open Default Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)).\n\n## Custom keyboard shortcuts for refactorings\n\nThe`editor.action.codeAction` command lets you configure keyboard shortcuts for specific [Refactorings](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editing/refactoring)(Code Actions). For example, the keyboard shortcut below triggers the Extract function refactoring Code Action:\n\n```\n{\n  \"key\": \"ctrl+shift+r ctrl+e\",\n  \"command\": \"editor.action.codeAction\",\n  \"args\": {\n    \"kind\": \"refactor.extract.function\"\n  }\n}\n\n```\n\nThis is covered in depth in the [Refactoring](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editing/refactoring#_keyboard-shortcuts-for-code-actions) article, where you can learn about different kinds of Code Actions and how to prioritize them in the case of multiple possible refactorings.\n\n## Related resources\n\n- [VS Code default keyboard shortcuts reference](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/reference/default-keybindings)\n\n## Common questions\n\n### How can I find out what command is bound to a specific key?\n\nIn the Keyboard Shortcuts editor, you can filter on specific keystrokes to see which commands are bound to which keys. In the following screenshot, you can see that Ctrl+Shift+P is bound to Show All Commands to bring up the Command Palette.\n\n### How to add a keyboard shortcut to an action, for example, add Ctrl+D to Delete Lines\n\nFind a rule that triggers the action in the Default Keyboard Shortcuts and write a modified version of it in your`keybindings.json` file:\n\n```\n// Original, in Default Keyboard Shortcuts\n{ \"key\": \"ctrl+shift+k\",          \"command\": \"editor.action.deleteLines\",\n                                     \"when\": \"editorTextFocus\" },\n// Modified, in User/keybindings.json, Ctrl+D now will also trigger this action\n{ \"key\": \"ctrl+d\",                \"command\": \"editor.action.deleteLines\",\n                                     \"when\": \"editorTextFocus\" },\n\n```\n\n### How can I add a keyboard shortcut for only certain file types?\n\nUse the`editorLangId` context key in your`when` clause:\n\n```\n{ \"key\": \"shift+alt+a\",           \"command\": \"editor.action.blockComment\",\n                                     \"when\": \"editorTextFocus && editorLangId == csharp\" },\n\n```\n\n### I have modified my keyboard shortcuts in keybindings.json; why don't they work?\n\nThe most common problem is a syntax error in the file. The VS Code docs don't list the exact terminal group commands. The "command not found" suggests Cursor either:
1. Doesn't register those commands (e.g. uses a forked terminal that doesn't have "groups")
2. Registers them under a different ID

The safest fix is to remove the two keybindings that reference the non-existent commands so the user doesn't get the error. We can either:

**If you specifically need “focus previous/next *group*”** (split panes) and Cursor does expose it under another ID, that ID will show up in that Keyboard Shortcuts search; you can then switch the bindings back to the group commands using the correct IDs.

## Observability and control over keybindings in VS Code / Cursor

### 1. See which command runs for each keypress (live logging)

Use **Developer: Toggle Keyboard Shortcuts Troubleshooting** so every keypress is logged: what key was resolved and which command ran (including the winning `when` and source).

- **How:** Command Palette (**Cmd+Shift+P**) → run **“Developer: Toggle Keyboard Shortcuts Troubleshooting”**.
- **Effect:** Logging is turned on and the **Output** panel shows the keybinding log. Press the key (e.g. **Tab** in an edamagit buffer); the log will show something like: “From N keybinding entries, matched \<commandId\>, when: \<when clause\>, source: \<built-in|User|Extension\>.”
- **Use case:** Confirm whether **Tab** is triggering “Magit Toggle Fold” or another command (e.g. Accept Inline Suggestion, Vim tab, etc.) and why.  
[Keyboard shortcuts for Visual Studio Code – Troubleshooting](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/keybindings)  
[Troubleshoot shortcuts not working (Stack Overflow)](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58946149/how-to-troubleshoot-some-shortcuts-not-working-properly-in-vscode)

### 2. See all bindings for one key (who’s shadowing whom)

- **Keyboard Shortcuts UI:** Open **Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts** (or **Cmd+K Cmd+S**). Search by key (e.g. type **tab**) to list every binding for that key, with **Command**, **Keybinding**, **When**, and **Source**.
- **Same keybindings:** Right‑click a row → **“Show Same Keybindings”** to see every rule that shares that key. That shows exactly which commands compete for **Tab** (e.g. Magit Toggle Fold, Accept Inline Suggestion, Vim, terminal accept, etc.).  
[Keyboard shortcuts for Visual Studio Code – Detecting conflicts](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/keybindings)

### 3. How VS Code picks the winning binding (so you can override)

Rules are evaluated **bottom to top**. The **first** rule that matches both the **key** and the **when** clause is used; no further rules are checked. User keybindings are appended on top of defaults, so your entries can override built‑in and extension bindings.  
[Keyboard shortcuts for Visual Studio Code – Keyboard rules](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/keybindings)

So for **Tab** in edamagit:

- If “Magit Toggle Fold” has a **narrow** `when` (e.g. `editorTextFocus && editorLangId == 'edamagit-cursor-c'`) and another **Tab** binding has a **broader** or earlier-matching `when`, the other one can win.
- To make Magit win, you need your **Magit Tab** rule to be the one that matches when you’re in edamagit (either by removing/narrowing the other rules or by adding a **User** rule with a specific enough `when`).

### 4. Overriding and unshadowing (give Magit Tab priority)

- **Remove a binding:** In **Keyboard Shortcuts**, right‑click the row you don’t want → **Remove Keybinding**. Or in `keybindings.json` add a **removal** rule: same `key`, command prefixed with `-`, e.g.  
  `{ "key": "tab", "command": "-acceptSelectedSuggestion", "when": "..." }`  
  to stop that specific rule from taking **Tab**.
- **Narrow another binding’s when:** Right‑click the row → **“Change When Expression”** and tighten the `when` so it doesn’t apply in edamagit (e.g. add `&& editorLangId != 'edamagit-cursor-c'` or the exact lang id you see in the UI).
- **Ensure Magit wins in edamagit:** Add a **User** keybinding in `keybindings.json` for **Tab** that calls the Magit Toggle Fold command with a `when` that is true **only** in edamagit (e.g. `editorTextFocus && editorLangId == 'edamagit-cursor-c'`). Because user rules are merged and evaluated with the rest, a specific `when` for edamagit will make Magit win when that context is active.  
[Keyboard shortcuts for Visual Studio Code – Removing a keybinding](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/keybindings)

### 5. Record Keys to capture the exact key and conflicts

Use **Record Keys** (keyboard icon next to the search in Keyboard Shortcuts, or **Option+Cmd+K** on Mac): press **Tab** (e.g. in an edamagit buffer). The UI will show **all** bindings for that key; you can see which one would fire in the current context and remove or change the ones that shadow Magit.  
[Troubleshoot shortcuts not working (Stack Overflow)](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58946149/how-to-troubleshoot-some-shortcuts-not-working-properly-in-vscode)

### 6. Optional: Inspect default keybinding JSON

Run **Preferences: Open Default Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)** from the Command Palette to open the default keybindings file. You can search for `tab` and see the exact `key`, `command`, and `when` for every built‑in and extension rule; useful to copy or adapt when writing overrides in your user `keybindings.json`.  
[Built-in Commands | VS Code Extension API](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/references/commands)

## Practical workflow for your Tab + Magit case

1. **Cmd+Shift+P** → **Developer: Toggle Keyboard Shortcuts Troubleshooting** → open Output and select the keybinding log.
2. Focus an edamagit buffer and press **Tab**. Note the “matched” command and its `when`/source.
3. **Cmd+K Cmd+S** → search **tab** → right‑click “Magit Toggle Fold” → **Show Same Keybindings**. Note which other **Tab** bindings have `when` clauses that could be true in edamagit (e.g. Accept Inline Suggestion, `extension.vim_tab`, etc.).
4. In **keybindings.json**, add a **removal** rule for the command that’s currently winning in edamagit (e.g. `-acceptSelectedSuggestion` or the exact id) with a `when` that includes being in edamagit so you only disable it there; **or** add a **User** binding for **Tab** → Magit Toggle Fold with `when": "editorTextFocus && editorLangId == 'edamagit-cursor-c'` (use the exact `editorLangId` shown in Keyboard Shortcuts for Magit).

That gives you full observability (troubleshooting log + “Show Same Keybindings”) and a clear way to override so “Magit Toggle Fold” gets **Tab** in edamagit.

Vim’s Tab binding (`extension.vim_tab`) is winning because its `when` clause matches in edamagit (editor focus, Vim active, not Insert mode). Magit Toggle Fold only runs when its own `when` matches; once Vim’s rule is chosen, Magit’s isn’t evaluated.

**Fix: remove Vim’s Tab binding in Magit/edamagit buffers**

Add a **removal** rule in your user `keybindings.json` so that in edamagit, Vim’s Tab binding is disabled and the next matching binding (Magit Toggle Fold) can run.

Use the **same `editorLangId`** that Magit uses. In your keybindings you already have both `editorLangId == 'magit'` and the screenshot showed `edamagit-cursor-c` for Magit Toggle Fold. Cover both so it works in every Magit buffer:

```json
{
  "key": "tab",
  "command": "-extension.vim_tab",
  "when": "editorTextFocus && (editorLangId == 'magit' || editorLangId == 'edamagit-cursor-c')"
}
```

**Where to add it**

- In [keybindings.json](keybindings.json): put this entry inside the existing array (e.g. near your other edamagit overrides around the magit/vim_tab block, ~lines 64–75).

**Why this works**

- Keybinding resolution picks the **first** matching rule (bottom-to-top in the merged list). User keybindings are appended and evaluated first.
- This rule **removes** `extension.vim_tab` only when `editorTextFocus` and the editor is a Magit buffer (`editorLangId` is `magit` or `edamagit-cursor-c`).
- In that context, Vim’s Tab no longer runs, so the next matching Tab binding (Magit Toggle Fold) is used.

**If Magit only uses one lang id**

If you’re sure all Magit buffers use a single language id, you can shorten to:

```json
"when": "editorTextFocus && editorLangId == 'magit'"
```

or

```json
"when": "editorTextFocus && editorLangId == 'edamagit-cursor-c'"
```

After editing `keybindings.json`, reload the window (**Developer: Reload Window**) or restart Cursor, then try Tab in an edamagit buffer again. The KeybindingService log should show the Magit command being invoked instead of `extension.vim_tab`.

_**User**_

outside of edamagit, what does vim usually do? what's its purpose?

---

_**Agent**_

The user is asking about what the Vim extension's Tab key does outside of edamagit - i.e. what is the purpose of `extension.vim_tab` in normal Vim usage. This is a conceptual question about VSCodeVim / Vim keybindings.

In Vim, the Tab key in Normal mode typically:
- Indents the current line (same as >> or :>
- Or in some configurations, can be used for completion or other motions

In VSCodeVim (the extension), `extension.vim_tab` is the command that gets triggered when you press Tab. It usually maps to Vim's normal Tab behavior - which in classic Vim is often "indent the current line" in Normal mode (or move to next tab stop in Insert mode; in Normal mode Tab often does indent). So the purpose is: when you're in a code editor with Vim mode active and not in Insert mode, Tab triggers the Vim-style Tab action (typically indent line or similar).

I don't need to edit anything - just answer from knowledge. I can also quickly check if the user's keybindings or any docs in the repo mention what vim_tab does.

---

_**Agent**_

Outside of edamagit, **Vim’s Tab** (the binding that runs `extension.vim_tab`) is doing the same thing the normal **Tab** key does in Vim when you’re in **Normal** (or other non-Insert) mode: it runs the Vim command that’s bound to `<Tab>` in that mode.

In typical Vim setups that’s **indenting**: in Normal mode, Tab usually inserts indent at the cursor (same idea as `>>` for the current line). So in a normal code buffer with the Vim extension, Tab is “indent this line / do Vim’s Tab action” instead of “insert a tab character” (which is Insert-mode behavior).

So the **purpose** of `extension.vim_tab` outside edamagit is: **run Vim’s Tab behavior** (usually indent) when the editor has focus, Vim is active, you’re not in Insert mode, and you’re not in a debug/inline-edit context. Your minimal removal only turns that off in Magit/edamagit buffers so Magit Toggle Fold can use Tab there; everywhere else Tab still does the usual Vim Tab (indent) thing.

_**Agent**_

Reverted to the stronger setup:

1. **Global remove** – `-extension.vim_tab` with no `when`, so the extension’s Tab binding is cleared everywhere.
2. **Re-add** – `extension.vim_tab` only when the usual Vim conditions hold **and** `!(editorLangId =~ /magit/)`, so any buffer whose language id contains `"magit"` is excluded.

So Tab in Magit/edamagit buffers is no longer handled by Vim and can go to Magit Toggle Fold; in all other buffers Vim still gets Tab for its normal behavior. Reload the window once and try again.

Here are the key commands available:[1]\n\n## Main Commands\n\n- **magit.status** - Opens the Magit status view (default: `Alt+X G`)\n- **magit.file-popup** - Opens file popup (default: `Alt+X Alt+G`)\n- **magit.dispatch** - Opens dispatch menu (default: `Alt+X Ctrl+G`)\n\n## Status View Actions\n\n- **magit.refresh** - Refresh current buffer\n- **magit.discard-at-point** - Discard changes/file/stash under cursor\n- **magit.reverse-at-point** - Reverse changes under cursor\n- **magit.reverting** - Reverting command\n\n## Core Git Operations\n\nWithin the status view, you can access additional commands through keyboard shortcuts:[1]\n- Stage/Unstage changes (`s`/`u`)\n- Apply changes (`a`)\n- Commit (`c`), branch (`b`), merge (`m`), rebase (`r`)\n- Push (`P`), pull (`F`), fetch (`f`)\n- Stash (`z`), tag (`t`), reset (`X`)\n\nYou can view all available magit commands by typing `> Magit` in the VSCode command palette.[1]"}],"isFinal":true,"rejected":false}
